steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper presenting CreativeConnect, a generative-AI system that helps graphic designers recombine reference images during ideation. Cover why recombination is useful but laborious, what earlier tools do and miss, our formative study and design goals, the system, the user study findings, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- References and recombination in creative design
- Effort required at each step of recombination
- Prior support tools and their gaps
- Formative study and design goals
- CreativeConnect system
- User study and findings
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- References and recombination
  - references crucial in creative thinking (e.g. graphic design): grasp existing ideas, ignite new ones
  - diverse visual, conceptual, functional stimuli; explore directions, learn from successful examples
  - combining existing examples = combinatorial creativity
  - reference recombination: extract elements/aspects from multiple references, consider connections, blend into novel ideas
- Effort
  - designers must dissect references into elements, analyze which combinations worth mixing
  - draw multiple sketches to find ways of blending
  - long, many iterations; harder for less experienced (identifying factors, integrating disparate domains) vs professionals
- Prior support
  - decompose references / show connections -> but no guidance on incorporating elements into a design
  - blending concepts/images -> precise, harmonious combinations, not diverse exploratory ones
  - search by genetic recombination -> widens exploration, no inspiration on combining specific elements
- Formative study + design goals
  - six early-stage graphic designers and design students
  - two stages: 1) conceptual ideation (convey topic), 2) visual ideation (style details); focus on conceptual (recombination more prevalent)
  - four element types: subject matter, action & pose, theme & mood, compositional aspects (arrangement)
  - brainstorm related elements, combine; manual effort high -> can't try all methods
  - support shouldn't be overly completed (diminishes own input)
  - goals: (1) effortless specification of four element types, (2) recommend relevant elements, (3) as many recombinations as possible, (4) output partially unfinished
- CreativeConnect
  - extract elements from reference images, generate wide range of recombinations
  - select elements by four types; recommendations of relevant keywords
  - recombination options as sketch image + one-line description pairs
  - pipelines with generative models: keyword extraction, recombination options, descriptions + sketches
- User study
  - within-subjects, 16 design students; baseline = mood board with manual keyword notes + layout diffusion model + ChatGPT
  - supports both stages (discovering elements, generating ideas)
  - more ideas in given time; perceived more creative sketches; ideas vastly different from initial concepts
  - compared creativity support; opportunity for comprehensive recombination tool
  - low-fidelity sketches -> more imagination, stimulus
  - generalizability: expertise, collaboration, design domains
- Contributions
  - (1) system; (2) computational pipelines; (3) user study findings (N=16)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
When doing creative work like graphic design, references are very important. They are a source both for understanding the landscape of existing ideas and for sparking new ones. References give diverse visual, conceptual, and functional stimuli, so people can explore different creative directions and learn from successful examples that already exist. One good way to come up with new ideas from references is to combine existing examples, and this is often called combinatorial creativity. In practice this is often done by reference recombination, which means extracting the elements or aspects from multiple references, thinking about the connections between them, and blending them to get novel design ideas.

But every step of recombination takes a lot of effort from designers. To find sources for recombination, designers have to dissect the references into individual elements and analyze them to decide which combinations of elements are worth mixing. They also have to explore by drawing many sketches to find good ways to blend the elements into a new design idea. This takes a long time and many iterations. It is especially hard for less experienced people, because compared to professionals they have difficulty identifying various factors from references and integrating references from disparate domains.

Previous research has supported these individual steps. Several approaches were proposed to decompose references or show the connections between them, which helps users identify sources for recombination. But these approaches do not guide how to put the extracted elements into a design. Many approaches have also tried to help users blend different concepts or images into a new one. However these mainly focus on generating precise combinations that incorporate all elements harmoniously, and not on producing diverse combinations for creative exploration. Another line of research is searching by genetic recombination. But these techniques focused on widening the range of design exploration, not on giving inspiration on how to effectively combine specific design elements.

- Formative study + design goals
  - six early-stage graphic designers and design students
  - two stages: conceptual ideation vs visual ideation; focus on conceptual
  - four element types: subject matter, action & pose, theme & mood, compositional aspects (arrangement)
  - manual recombination effortful; support shouldn't be overly completed
  - four design goals: specify elements, recommend elements, many recombinations, partially unfinished output
- CreativeConnect
  - extract elements by four types + keyword recommendations
  - recombination options as sketch + one-line description pairs
  - generative-model pipelines for extraction, recombination, descriptions, sketches
- User study
  - within-subjects, 16 design students; baseline: mood board + manual keyword notes, layout diffusion model, ChatGPT
  - supports both stages; more ideas; more creative sketches; ideas far from initial concepts
  - comprehensive tool opportunity; low fidelity sketches stimulate imagination; generalizability
- Contributions: (1) system, (2) pipelines, (3) user study findings (N=16)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When doing creative work like graphic design, references are very important. They are a source both for understanding the landscape of existing ideas and for sparking new ones. References give diverse visual, conceptual, and functional stimuli, so people can explore different creative directions and learn from successful examples that already exist. One good way to come up with new ideas from references is to combine existing examples, and this is often called combinatorial creativity. In practice this is often done by reference recombination, which means extracting the elements or aspects from multiple references, thinking about the connections between them, and blending them to get novel design ideas.

But every step of recombination takes a lot of effort from designers. To find sources for recombination, designers have to dissect the references into individual elements and analyze them to decide which combinations of elements are worth mixing. They also have to explore by drawing many sketches to find good ways to blend the elements into a new design idea. This takes a long time and many iterations. It is especially hard for less experienced people, because compared to professionals they have difficulty identifying various factors from references and integrating references from disparate domains.

Previous research has supported these individual steps. Several approaches were proposed to decompose references or show the connections between them, which helps users identify sources for recombination. But these approaches do not guide how to put the extracted elements into a design. Many approaches have also tried to help users blend different concepts or images into a new one. However these mainly focus on generating precise combinations that incorporate all elements harmoniously, and not on producing diverse combinations for creative exploration. Another line of research is searching by genetic recombination. But these techniques focused on widening the range of design exploration, not on giving inspiration on how to effectively combine specific design elements.

We ran a formative study with six early-stage graphic designers and design students to understand the process of reference recombination and find their challenges. We saw two distinct stages of ideation: 1) conceptual ideation, which aims to convey the design topic effectively, and 2) visual ideation, which is deciding style-wise details on top of the selected concept. We decided to focus on conceptual ideation since recombination of references tends to happen more in this stage. During conceptual ideation, designers extracted four types of elements from the reference: subject matter, action & pose, theme & mood, and compositional aspects (arrangement). Then they brainstormed more elements related to the extracted ones and combined them in several ways. But recombining manually takes high effort, so they were worried they could not try out all possible methods. They also said that support for ideation should not be in a too complete form, because it can diminish their own input. From these observations we propose four design goals for a system that supports reference recombination: (1) let users effortlessly specify the four types of conceptual elements from the reference image, (2) recommend relevant elements, (3) provide as many recombinations as possible, and (4) intentionally keep the generated output partially unfinished to foster the user's creativity.

Based on these design goals we propose CreativeConnect. It is a system that supports the design ideation process by helping users easily extract elements from reference images and generate a wide range of recombinations of the elements. With CreativeConnect users can discover and select elements from the reference image based on the four element types, and get recommendations of more relevant keywords. When the user has chosen the keywords to combine, they get various recombination options shown as pairs of sketch images and one-line descriptions. We introduced new pipelines with generative models that automate extracting keywords from images, generating recombination options, and turning them into descriptions and sketches.

We did a within-subjects study with 16 design students that compared CreativeConnect with a baseline system. The baseline was a mood board with manual keyword notes, a layout diffusion model, and ChatGPT. The results showed that CreativeConnect could support both stages of the reference recombination process, which are discovering elements from references and generating design ideas by recombining them. Participants also produced more design ideas in the given time, and they felt that CreativeConnect helped them make more creative sketches than the baseline. They said CreativeConnect was especially helpful for getting inspirational ideas that were very different from their initial concepts. We compared the creativity support of CreativeConnect and the baseline, and we proposed an opportunity to design a comprehensive recombination support tool that could support a broad range of design needs and situations. We also found that because the sketch-based output was low fidelity, users imagined more and got more stimulus for their creativity. Finally we discussed how CreativeConnect generalizes in terms of user expertise, collaborative settings, and different domains of design.

The contributions of this paper are:

- (1) CreativeConnect, a system that supports the ideation process of graphic designers by helping extract elements from reference images and suggesting a wide range of recombinations of those elements.

- (2) Computational pipelines with generative models that extract and suggest keywords from images and generate recombinations of keywords as text descriptions and sketches.

- (3) Findings from a user study (N=16) on how CreativeConnect helps designers in each step of recombination, which led to more design ideas and to participants perceiving their ideas as more creative.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
References play a crucial role in creative thinking such as graphic design, serving as valuable sources both for grasping the landscape of existing ideas and for igniting novel ones [1,2,3,4]. They offer diverse visual, conceptual, and functional stimuli, allowing individuals to explore various creative directions and draw lessons from established successful examples [5]. One effective way to generate new ideas from references is to combine existing examples, often called combinatorial creativity [6,7,8,9]. In practice, this is often done through reference recombination: extracting the elements or aspects of multiple references, considering the connections between them [1], and blending them to gain novel design ideas [10].

However, each step of recombination requires significant effort from designers. To discover sources for recombination, designers need to dissect references into individual elements and analyze them to determine which combinations are worth mixing. They must also engage in exploration, drawing multiple sketches to find effective ways of blending those elements into a new design idea. This takes a long time and multiple iterations, especially for those less experienced in the design process, who have more difficulty than professionals in identifying various factors from references and integrating references from disparate domains [11].

Previous research has provided support for these individual steps. Several approaches have been proposed [12,13,14] to decompose references or show connections between them, aiding users in identifying sources for recombination. However, these approaches do not guide how to incorporate the extracted elements into a design. Many approaches have also attempted to help users blend different concepts or images into a novel one [15,16,17,18]. However, these primarily emphasize generating precise combinations that incorporate all elements harmoniously, rather than producing diverse combinations for creative exploration. Another thread of research focuses on searching by genetic recombination [19,20,21,22]. Still, these techniques focus on widening the range of design exploration rather than offering inspiration on how to effectively combine specific design elements.

Through a formative study with six early-stage graphic designers and design students, we aimed to understand the process of reference recombination and identify their challenges. We observed two distinctive stages of ideation: 1) conceptual ideation, which aims to convey the design topic effectively, and 2) visual ideation, which is about deciding style-wise details on top of the selected concept. We focused on the conceptual stage, as recombination of references tends to be more prevalent there. During conceptual ideation, designers extracted four types of elements from the reference—subject matter, action & pose, theme & mood, and compositional aspects (arrangement). They then tried to brainstorm more elements related to the extracted ones and combine them in several ways. However, because recombining them manually required high effort, they were concerned that they could not try out all possible methods. They also mentioned that ideation support should not come in an overly completed form, as this can diminish their own input. With these observations, we propose four design goals for a reference recombination support system: (1) enable users to effortlessly specify the four types of conceptual elements from the reference image, (2) recommend relevant elements, (3) provide as many recombinations as possible, and (4) intentionally keep the generated output partially unfinished to foster the user’s creativity.

Based on these design goals, we propose CreativeConnect, a system that supports the design ideation process by helping users easily extract elements from reference images and generate a wide range of recombinations of those elements. Using CreativeConnect, users can discover and select elements from the reference image based on the four element types and receive recommendations for more relevant keywords. Once the user has chosen the keywords to combine, they get various recombination options presented as pairs of sketch images and one-line descriptions. We introduced novel pipelines with generative models to automate the extraction of keywords from images, generate recombination options, and transform them into descriptions and sketches.

We conducted a within-subjects study with 16 design students comparing CreativeConnect with a baseline system consisting of a mood board with manual keyword notes, a layout diffusion model, and ChatGPT. Results showed that CreativeConnect could support both stages of the reference recombination process: discovering elements from references and generating design ideas by recombining them. Participants also produced more design ideas in a given time and perceived that CreativeConnect helped them develop more creative sketches than the baseline. They emphasized that CreativeConnect was especially beneficial for getting inspirational ideas vastly different from their initial concepts. We compared the creativity support of CreativeConnect with that of the baseline and proposed an opportunity to design a comprehensive recombination support tool for a broad spectrum of design needs and situations. We also found that the low fidelity of the sketch-based output led users to imagine more and gave more stimulus for their creativity. Finally, we discussed the generalizability of CreativeConnect in terms of user expertise, collaborative settings, and different design domains.

This paper presents the following contributions:

- (1) CreativeConnect, a system that supports graphic designers’ ideation process by helping them extract elements from reference images and suggesting a wide range of recombinations of those elements.

- (2) Computational pipelines with generative models that extract and suggest keywords from images and generate recombinations of keywords as text descriptions and sketches.

- (3) Findings from a user study (N=16) about how CreativeConnect aids designers in each step of recombination, leading to more design ideas and to participants perceiving their ideas as more creative.
